transcript:
Header: 2026-10-21 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Location: Zoom
Attendees: Elliot Park (Redwood AE), Rina Gupta (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (NexaHealth Head of ML), Daniel Kim (NexaHealth Infra Engineer), Marisol Vega (NexaHealth SRE)

Summary: Technical deep dive on throughput tuning for Redwood runtime. Covered continuous batching, scheduler knobs (latency-first vs throughput-first), max_num_seqs, token limits, KV cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem considerations. Agreed to run a staged benchmark and share a perf runbook and kernel notes.

Topics: continuous batching; scheduler knobs; max_num_seqs; token limits and truncation; KV cache eviction & prefix caching; quantization impacts; dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs; on-prem/VPC networking concerns.

[00:00] Elliot: ok everyone thanks for jumping on, we're gonna dive into throughput tuning — I think the ask from Priya was mostly around improving p95 for our short chat workload while keeping token costs low.
[00:18] Priya: yeah that's right, hi all. Our median seq len is like 24 tokens but we have a long tail to 512 occasionally, and p95 latency is our blocker for user-facing apps.
[00:30] Rina: cool, that distribution is actually a common pattern, we see short sequences majority + occasional long. There's a few levers: continuous batching, scheduler policy, and configuring max_num_seqs on the worker to favor packing.
[00:45] Daniel: quick q, what's max_num_seqs exactly? we saw it in the readme but not sure how it interacts with KV cache.
[00:52] Rina: good q — max_num_seqs caps how many concurrent sequences the GPU worker will pack into a single micro-batch for decoding steps. It directly affects throughput: higher value -> more packing -> higher token/sec for short sequences. But it increases prefill memory (KV cache) and can add buildup latency while waiting to fill the pack.
[01:12] Marisol: so it's a latency vs throughput tradeoff, right; if we push it too high p95 gets worse on cold arrivals.
[01:18] Elliot: exactly. Scheduler knobs let you choose policy: latency-first uses small windows and lower max_num_seqs, throughput-first increases batching windows and packs aggressively. You can also do dynamic switching based on load.
[01:30] Priya: can you give real numbers? like what we'd expect on a T4/RTX or A100?
[01:36] Rina: rough ballpark — on an A100, going from max_num_seqs=8 to 32 for short seqs can 2-3x tokens/sec for the packed workload, but cold latency for singleton requests may see 10-30ms extra scheduling delay. On a T4 it's similar direction but smaller multiplier. Also quantization changes op throughput — 4-bit kernels can be 1.8x-2.5x faster for matmuls but accuracy regression depends on model and prompt sensitivity.
[02:05] Daniel: and KV cache memory when we bump max_num_seqs, is that linear? Our on-prem nodes have 96GB GPU mem per box.
[02:13] Rina: KV scales roughly with num_tokens * hidden_size * bytes_per_param * max_num_seqs factor for packed sequences — so yes more packed seqs and longer sequences -> more KV. If you quantize weight/activations you can reduce memory pressure too, but quantized KV support varies per kernel.
[02:30] Priya: what about prefill vs decode — we do streaming decode for chat, how does batching behave?
[02:36] Rina: we separate prefill (encoder/prompt) and decode. Prefill is expensive but easy to batch; continuous batching mostly targets decode-time packing across multiple live requests. For streaming chat you want low decode latency so smaller decode batch windows, but then you lose throughput. There's also prefix caching — if many users share the same system prompt or context, we can serve from KV cache to avoid repeated prefill cost.
[02:58] Elliot: quick interjection — we can enable smart prefix caching for their LLM routes; Daniel if you can share common prompt fingerprints we'll show cache hit improvements in the benchmark.
[03:07] Daniel: noted. We'll export distribution.
[03:10] [03:10] Priya: can you explain the scheduler knobs in config? we have a running Dedicated pool and don't want to change runtime code.
[03:18] Rina: in Dedicated you can set per-route scheduling policy: window_ms (how long the scheduler waits for more requests), max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_batch, and mode (latency|throughput|adaptive). Adaptive mode tries to balance by shortening windows at low QPS and lengthening during bursts.
[03:35] Marisol: how does adaptive decide thresholds? is it reactive to observed p95?
[03:40] Rina: yes it's reactive: it tracks queue length, average fill rate, and recent latency metrics. There are knobs for target latency percentiles and hysteresis. We'll share the default heuristics in the runbook.
[03:52] Priya: what about token limits — right now our requests get truncated at 1024 tokens, should we increase?
[03:58] Elliot: increasing token limit means larger prefill cost and KV cache pressure; if most requests are small it's wasted. Better approach: set per-route token cap matching the business need and use streaming truncation for long tails. For training-like workloads you'd raise limits, but for chat user-facing flows stick to conservative caps.
[04:20] Daniel: network overhead — we're on VPC private deployment (redwood private) — will batching across instances introduce cross-node traffic?
[04:28] Rina: batching is per-worker process; we don't micro-batch across independent hosts unless you're using a sharded multi-GPU worker. In dedicated pools each worker packs requests it receives locally. Cross-host routing may happen if load balancer forwards to different workers, but that doesn't cause inter-GPU KV traffic. On multi-GPU sharded models, KV is local to the shard and we coordinate, but that's a different path and needs RDMA/NCCL tuned.
[04:50] Marisol: ok good — our infra constraints are we cannot open RDMA between certain racks, so we avoid sharded workers; we prefer single-GPU workers.
[04:58] Rina: single-GPU workers simplifies batching and reduces cross-host complexity, but you lose some throughput for very large models. For your seq lengths single-GPU is fine.
[05:08] [05:08] Priya: on quantization — you mentioned 4-bit kernels — any accuracy numbers?
[05:13] Rina: depends on model and eval set. For base open models we've seen 1-3% drop on some benchmarks moving to 4-bit asymmetric quantization, often imperceptible for chat. We recommend running evals on your prompt suite. Also some LLM ops (layernorm, softmax) are sensitive; Redwood's kernel selector will prefer higher-precision path for those ops if the model requires it.
[05:33] Elliot: note: we can provide quantization profiles tuned for your model and prompt set as part of the pilot.
[05:38] Daniel: if we enable quantization and increased max_num_seqs, can we run into correctness issues due to KV quantization mismatch?
[05:45] Rina: we avoid quantizing KV caches by default; quantization primarily applies to weights and compute kernels. That preserves numerical stability of cached keys/values. Some experimental configs do quantized KV, but they're opt-in.
[05:58] Marisol: what about eviction policy for KV cache? if we cache prefixes across many users, when do entries expire?
[06:05] Rina: TTL-based plus LRU heuristics. You can tune per-route TTL and max cache size. Also cache keys are fingerprinted on route+prompt-hash+customer id so you keep isolation.
[06:18] Priya: ok that helps. Transitioning, can you walk through a proposed benchmark plan?
[06:23] Elliot: we'll run three phases: 1) baseline with your current config; 2) apply throughput-first scheduler with higher max_num_seqs and 4-bit quantization on a staging worker; 3) run mixed workload to measure p50/p95/p99 and token/sec and cost delta. We'll also test adaptive mode.
[06:38] Daniel: for phase 2 we'd like to replicate our traffic pattern including the 512-token tail. How do you recommend modeling that?
[06:44] Rina: provide a histogram of sequence lengths and arrival rates; we'll use a Poisson arrival generator with a heavy-tail distribution to mimic your spikes. For decode we simulate streaming steps for short seqs and full prefill for long seqs.
[06:58] Elliot: we'll also include prefix cache hit scenarios (0%, 30%, 70%) to show sensitivity.
[07:05] Priya: any config sample you can share now?
[07:08] Rina: yes, sample snippet: window_ms=15 for latency-first, window_ms=60-120 for throughput-first; max_num_seqs defaults 8, throughput tuning try 24-32; max_tokens_per_batch depends on GPU mem, often 4096-16384. We'll send exact values mapped to NVIDIA GPU types.
[07:28] Marisol: 15ms wait sounds small — is that the scheduler polling interval?
[07:31] Rina: it's the maximum wait time the scheduler will hold an unfilled batch before flushing; actual fill time may be shorter if enough requests arrive.
[07:40] Daniel: curious about billing implications — if we pack more requests do you meter differently?
[07:45] Elliot: for Hosted we meter tokens; packing only affects per-token cost via more efficient runtime. For Dedicated you pay reserved capacity; we track token-level and per-route breakdowns in Console so you can analyze unit economics.
[07:58] [08:00] Priya: are there safety/confidentiality concerns with KV cache when multiple customers use the same worker?
[08:05] Rina: KV cache entries are partitioned by tenant and route, with strict isolation. For Dedicated we can enforce worker-level tenancy so no cross-tenant sharing. We also log cache accesses in audit logs if you need them.
[08:18] Priya: good. Also please include SOC2 artifact when you send security docs.
[08:22] Elliot: will do.
[08:25] [08:25] Rina: deeper nitty-gritty — scheduler also supports max_wait_per_request_ms to prevent starvation; and you can set min_fill_rate so the scheduler doesn't block below a throughput threshold. These help balance tail latency.
[08:40] Daniel: about kernel selection — is that automatic in Redwood runtime? can we lock to a particular kernel set?
[08:46] Rina: automatic by default: the compiler chooses kernels by model arch, seq len distribution, and hardware. You can pin kernel profiles per model for reproducibility in production. We'll include the kernel export so you can match staging exactly to prod.
[08:58] Priya: what about telemetry — we need per-route traces showing queue time, prefill time, decode time, kernel time.
[09:05] Elliot: Console provides per-route breakdown with token-level cost, queue vs decode latencies, and per-kernel timing for deeper traces. We can expose custom traces to your S3 or datadog if needed.
[09:18] Marisol: for on-prem, we need the console private control plane — that's available?
[09:22] Rina: yes Redwood Private provides a customer-controlled control plane and can push metrics to your monitoring endpoints; we support SAML SSO, KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs.
[09:33] [09:33] Priya: ok great. Let's talk about a concrete tuning recommendation for our chat route given our short median seq and occasional long tail.
[09:40] Rina: recommendation: set route to adaptive mode with target p95=220ms; baseline window_ms=30, scale window_ms up to 100 under high queue; set max_num_seqs=24 for staging trial; set max_tokens_per_batch=8192; enable prefix caching with TTL=12h for system prompts; enable 4-bit quantization for weights but keep KV in fp16; run for 48h with 0/30/70% prefix hit scenarios.
[10:05] Daniel: sounds good — how safe is 4-bit on our model? we use open 7B variant.
[10:11] Rina: 7B usually tolerates 4-bit well but we will run your eval prompt set; if regression > threshold we can fallback to fp16 kernel for sensitive ops.
[10:20] Priya: and rollout strategy? we don't want to degrade prod.
[10:23] Elliot: canary rollouts per route: start with 5% traffic through tuned worker, monitor p95 and quality regressions, then 20%, 50%. Redwood supports automatic rollback on quality or latency regressions.
[10:34] Marisol: what thresholds trigger rollback?
[10:37] Rina: configurable, default is 5% regression on your configured eval metric or 20% p95 increase vs baseline for >5 minutes. We'll share the exact defaults.
[10:47] [10:47] Daniel: a couple of edge cases — long-running streams that never finish, do they hold KV forever?
[10:52] Rina: we terminate idle sessions after configurable TTL (default 30m) and evict associated KV; long-running active streams count against active sessions and need careful capacity planning.
[11:03] Priya: ok, one more question: can we pre-warm cache for known high-traffic prefixes before peak windows?
[11:08] Rina: yes, we have cache prefill APIs and synthetic warmers. We'll include a script you can run in perf runbook.
[11:14] Elliot: great — we're at about 40 minutes in, any other blockers?
[11:18] Priya: timeline: we'd like to run pilot next week and decide on Dedicated commit in three weeks.
[11:23] Elliot: sounds feasible. We'll send runbook and propose times.
[11:27] Marisol: for Dedicated, we need documentation on network lockdown and KMS integration too.
[11:31] Elliot: will include.
[11:34] [11:34] Rina: to close, quick troubleshooting tips: if p95 worsens after increasing max_num_seqs, lower window_ms first, then reduce max_num_seqs; check cache hit rate, and verify kernel choices (pin to fp16 for sensitive ops).
[11:50] Priya: perfect.
[11:52] Elliot: recap of next steps: 1) Elliot share perf runbook + kernel notes; 2) Rina propose default scheduler knobs and config sample; 3) Daniel provide seq length histogram and target SLAs; 4) schedule benchmark next week.
[12:05] Priya: thanks all.
[12:07] Meeting end.
